beginner: Spinach likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but drains well, with lots of compost mixed in. The one thing it really cares about is not-too-acidic soil, so if your ground is very acidic, add a little lime to bring it closer to neutral. A quick soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Spinach does best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. Its defining soil need is a near-neutral pH: spinach is notably sensitive to acidic soil and grows poorly below about 6.0, so lime an acid plot up toward 6.5 to 7.5 before sowing. Work in compost to feed the fast leafy growth and hold steady moisture, which delays bolting and keeps the leaves tender.

beginner: Spinach grows best in soil that is close to neutral, about 6.5 to 7.5. It does not like acidic soil, so if a soil test reads below 6.0, mix in some lime before planting.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.5 to 7.5; spinach is one of the more acid-sensitive vegetables and yields drop on soils below roughly 6.0, where manganese can become available enough to injure the plant. Clemson advises a 6.0 to 7.0 minimum and the University of Minnesota up to about 8, so lean to the neutral-to-slightly-alkaline side and lime an acid plot the season before.

beginner: Spinach grows fast and likes nitrogen for big green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after the seeds come up. Because the crop is quick, you usually do not need to feed it more than that.
seasoned: Spinach is a fast leafy crop that runs on nitrogen, but the season is short, so one or two feedings are usually enough. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting (or at thinning) to push tender, dark-green leaves. Utah State suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row; Clemson uses calcium nitrate. Avoid heavy late feeding, since spinach readily takes up nitrate and lush growth draws aphids and leafminers.

beginner: Time to give your spinach a feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your spinach with nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once the plants are a few weeks old.
seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 ft of row, or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), side-dressed 3 to 4 weeks after sowing. No phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one feeding a few weeks after the seeds sprout.
seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 (or 1 pound of calcium nitrate per 100 square feet) side-dressed once, 3 to 4 weeks after sowing.

beginner: Spinach is small, fast, and shade-tolerant, so it tucks in well between slower, taller crops. It grows happily next to peas and beans, strawberries, and members of the cabbage family, and it does not get along badly with much. Just keep it away from its close relatives beets and chard, which share its leafminer pest.
seasoned: Most spinach companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: spinach is shallow-rooted, quick, and tolerates light shade, so it interplants under or beside taller, slower crops (peas, beans, brassicas) and is harvested before they crowd it. The one well-grounded caution is to separate spinach from beets and Swiss chard, its close relatives in the goosefoot family, which share the spinach leafminer and several diseases, a rotation and pest principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Peas grow up while spinach stays low, so they share a bed without competing, and both love the same cool weather. Peas also add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy spinach can use.
seasoned: Peas and spinach are a traditional cool-season pairing on structure and timing: peas trellis upward and cast light shade that suits spinach, both thrive in the same early-spring and fall windows, and the legume fixes a little nitrogen the leafy spinach can draw on. Expect efficient use of the bed and season rather than a documented growth boost.

beginner: Strawberries and spinach are a long-standing garden pairing. The low spinach fills space between strawberry plants early in the season and is picked before the berries take over.
seasoned: Strawberries and spinach are a traditional pairing that works mainly on habit and timing: low, quick spinach uses the open ground between young strawberry plants in the cool of spring and is harvested before the berries spread. A space-use tradition, not a measured effect.

beginner: Tall cabbage-family plants give spinach a bit of light shade in warm spells, which helps it last longer before bolting, and the quick spinach is gone before the brassicas need the room.
seasoned: Spinach interplants beneath cabbage-family crops on a space-and-light basis: it tolerates the partial shade taller brassicas cast, which can buy a little time against bolting in warm spells, and it matures and is cleared before the brassicas fill out. Traditional and practical rather than a documented adjacency effect; the two do not share a major pest.

beginner: Keep spinach away from beets and Swiss chard. They are close relatives and share the same leafminer pest and some diseases, so planting them together helps those problems build up.
seasoned: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach all belong to the goosefoot family and are the favored hosts of the spinach leafminer, whose maggots blister and ruin the leaves; they also share several leaf diseases. Planting them side by side or in succession concentrates the leafminer and disease pressure and lets the soil-overwintering leafminer build. Separate them in space and rotate so goosefoot crops do not follow one another.

beginner: You'll see pale, winding tunnels in the leaves that widen into large tan blisters or blotches. If you hold a leaf up to the light, you can sometimes see the tiny maggot inside. The damaged parts are not good to eat.
seasoned: Slender, winding mines in the foliage enlarge into translucent tan blotches; heavily mined leaves are unmarketable and the crop is the leaf, so even light feeding matters. The pale legless maggots are visible inside the leaf against the light.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs on the underside of the leaves, and the maggots that hatch tunnel inside the leaf between the top and bottom layers, eating as they go. Spinach, beets, and chard are its favorites.
seasoned: The spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami) overwinters as pupae in the soil and emerges around mid-May; females lay rows of white eggs on leaf undersides, and the maggots tunnel between the leaf surfaces. There are three to four overlapping generations a season on spinach, beets, chard, and goosefoot weeds.

beginner: Once a maggot is inside a leaf, sprays do not reach it well, so pick off and destroy mined leaves as soon as you see them, before the maggots drop to the soil. Crushing the maggot inside the leaf works too.
seasoned: Insecticides poorly reach larvae inside the leaf, so rely on cultural control: pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate, and crush maggots in the leaf. Spinosad has some activity on young larvae; abamectin is a conventional option.

beginner: Cover the plants with a light row cover right after sowing so the flies cannot lay eggs, and pull nearby weeds like lambsquarters that host the pest. Rotating where you grow spinach, beets, and chard each year also helps.
seasoned: Exclude the egg-laying flies with floating row cover or insect netting from sowing, control goosefoot weeds (lambsquarters, chickweed, nightshade) that host the pest, rotate away from where spinach, beets, or chard grew, and deep-cultivate in spring to bury overwintering pupae.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, sometimes with curled, puckered leaves and a sticky coating. They are hard to wash out of crinkled savoy leaves.
seasoned: Colonies of green peach or other aphids on leaf undersides and growing tips distort and pucker the foliage; honeydew and sooty mold downgrade the crop, and curly savoy leaves are hard to clean. Aphids also transmit cucumber mosaic and other viruses.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on spinach; they reproduce rapidly, favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces, and are most damaging as virus vectors.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days until they are gone.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen fertilizer, and check the new growth often so you catch them early.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and use row cover, which doubles as leafminer exclusion.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Heavy damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Small round shot-holes pepper the leaves of young plants; the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Damage is mostly cosmetic on a leaf crop but can stunt or kill seedlings at high pressure.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little holes in young leaves. They hurt small seedlings the most, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young spinach and are most damaging at the seedling stage; the holes mar the harvested leaves.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are many beetles use a spinosad spray or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to shrug it off.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the aim is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Use row cover from sowing, keep seedlings strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and clear weeds nearby.
seasoned: Row cover from sowing, vigorous seedlings kept evenly watered and fed, and clean cultivation of nearby weeds.

beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green or striped caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. They are mostly a warm-season and southern problem.
seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; cabbage loopers, beet armyworms, and corn earworms feed on spinach, mostly in warm-season and southern plantings.

beginner: Several moths lay eggs on the leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch chew the foliage. Because you eat the leaves, even a little chewing is a problem.
seasoned: The larvae of several moths feed on spinach foliage; on a leaf crop even modest defoliation reduces the harvest.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them off by hand. Spray again after rain since it washes off.
seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad targeting young larvae, and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain.

beginner: Use a row cover, clean up old plants and weeds where moths shelter, and check the undersides of leaves for eggs and small caterpillars.
seasoned: Use row cover, clean up crop debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

beginner: Pale yellow patches on the tops of the leaves with a fuzzy gray-purple mold on the undersides, mostly in cool, damp, crowded conditions. Bad cases yellow and collapse the leaves.
seasoned: Irregular pale-yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface with grayish-purple sporulation beneath (the blue mold), spreading in cool, wet, humid weather; lesions brown and the leaves collapse. It is the most important spinach disease.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the same cool, wet weather spinach grows in, and spreads through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
seasoned: Peronospora effusa, an oomycete favored by cool temperatures, long leaf wetness, and high humidity; it spreads by wind- and splash-borne spores and survives on debris and as oospores, with many physiological races that overcome resistance.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the airflow so leaves dry faster, and water at the soil instead of over the plants. It is hard to stop once it gets going, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Cultural control dominates: improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected leaves and debris; copper has limited efficacy. There is no rescue once it is established in humid weather.

beginner: Grow resistant varieties (this is the main defense), space plants for good airflow, water at the base, and rotate where you plant spinach each year.
seasoned: Plant resistant cultivars (the primary tool, choosing the broadest race resistance available), widen spacing for airflow, use drip rather than overhead water, and rotate away from spinach for several years.

beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A serious disease in the southern and south-central states.

beginner: A different mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on the leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a crop quickly.
seasoned: The oomycete Albugo occidentalis, favored by cool nights, warm days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris.

beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.

beginner: Choose resistant varieties where it is common, space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, and rotate your planting spot.
seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from spinach.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where germination is slow.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up. Spinach sown in cold wet ground is at risk.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium species attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows emergence favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention. Pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No cure once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant at the right depth in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up fast.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil when temperatures favor quick emergence, avoid overwatering, use fresh viable seed, and consider treated seed where damping-off is chronic.

beginner: Older leaves yellow and wilt even though the soil is moist, and the wilting spreads up the plant, which is stunted and may die. It is worse in warm soil.
seasoned: Progressive yellowing and wilting from the lower leaves upward despite adequate soil moisture, with stunting and plant death; symptoms intensify as soil warms through the season.

beginner: A soil fungus infects the roots and clogs the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and yellows. It lives in the soil for years and is worse when the soil warms up.
seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. spinaciae, a soilborne vascular pathogen that persists for years and is favored by warm soil and acidic conditions; once established it limits where spinach can be grown.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected, so pull and destroy wilted plants. Put your effort into rotation and timing for next time.
seasoned: No effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants and manage the soilborne population by rotation and timing.

beginner: Plant spinach in the cooler parts of the season, keep the soil near neutral (not acidic), and do not grow spinach in the same spot year after year. Resistant varieties help where it is a problem.
seasoned: Schedule the crop for the cool side of the season when soils are cooler, maintain a near-neutral pH, use long rotations away from spinach, and choose resistant cultivars where the wilt is established.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even; spinach is shallow-rooted and bolts faster under drought stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week (Utah State cites 1 to 2 inches), more in warm, dry spells.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks downy mildew and white rust.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and leaves get moldy in soggy, crowded beds.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and downy mildew in crowded, constantly wet plantings.

beginner: Wilting leaves and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and faster bolting; drought stress is a direct bolt trigger in spinach.

beginner: Keep the soil damp and cool while spinach sprouts. It comes up poorly in warm soil.
seasoned: Spinach germinates best in cool, moist soil; keep the surface damp, since warm soil gives poor, patchy germination.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp. Spinach roots are shallow and dry out fast.
seasoned: Keep the seedlings evenly moist; spinach is shallow-rooted with little drought buffer.

beginner: Water evenly, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, as the leaves grow.
seasoned: Hold even moisture through leaf growth at about 1 to 1.5 inches a week; steady water builds thick, tender leaves.

beginner: Keep the water steady while you pick leaves, and give extra attention in warm weather. If spinach dries out it bolts (flowers) sooner and the harvest ends.
seasoned: Steady moisture through the leaf-bulking weeks, and especially through any warm, lengthening-day spell, delays bolt; spinach bolts faster under drought stress. Cut outer leaves and keep it watered to stretch the harvest.

beginner: When spinach sends up a flower stalk the leaves turn bitter, and watering will not fix it. Pull it and resow when it is cool.
seasoned: Once warmth and long days push it to bolt, the leaves turn bitter and arrow-shaped and watering will not reverse it. Pull and resow in cool weather.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the plants grow fast and tender and do not bolt early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps spinach growing fast and tender and delays bolting; dry spells push it to flower and turn the leaves bitter.

seasoned: Steady moisture through the leaf-bulking weeks and during any warm, lengthening-day spell matters most for delaying bolt.

beginner: Spinach is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows quickly and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop. The seeds sprout even in cold soil, but they will not come up well in hot soil, so do not sow in the heat of summer.
seasoned: Spinach is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring (it germinates in soil as cool as 40°F), and again in late summer for the main fall crop. Transplanting is possible from cells or soil blocks for an early start or to place an overwintering crop, but handle the roots gently. Germination is poor in soil above about 75 to 85°F, so summer sowings in warm regions wait for cooling soil.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients, and a little lime if your mix is acidic.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a starter nitrogen source; spinach dislikes acidity, so a pinch of lime helps if the mix is peat-heavy and acidic.

beginner: Shallow pots dry out fast, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Shallow containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress triggers bolting.

beginner: Feed a little more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container spinach needs slightly more frequent light feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown spinach can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
seasoned: Spinach is very cold-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming growth in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so sink it, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; an overwintered pot then yields the earliest spring picking.

beginner: Spinach grows well in a wide, shallow pot at least 6 inches deep, sown thickly and thinned for baby leaves or spaced for full plants. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it some afternoon shade in warm weather.
seasoned: Spinach is a good container crop because it is shallow-rooted, compact, and quick. Use a broad container at least 6 inches deep, one gallon or more, sown densely for cut baby leaves or thinned to 3 to 4 inches for full plants, and keep moisture even since shallow pots dry fast. Grow it in the cool seasons and give afternoon shade in warm spells to slow bolting.

seasoned: A self-watering container suits spinach well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and delays bolting.

beginner: Spinach has shallow roots, so a wide, shallow pot is better than a tall narrow one. Aim for at least 6 inches deep and as much width as you can give it.
seasoned: Spinach is shallow-rooted, so depth matters less than surface area: a wide, shallow container at least 6 inches deep gives more sowing area for cut-and-come-again leaves and buffers the fast drying narrow pots suffer.

beginner: Do not leave spinach out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Spinach wilts and yellows within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.

beginner: Store spinach unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it keeps for 1 to 2 weeks if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; spinach holds about 1 to 2 weeks near 32°F at high humidity. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds breakdown, so wait to wash until use.

beginner: Spinach freezes well if you blanch it first. Boil the leaves for about 2 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
seasoned: Spinach freezes well once blanched: dunk leaves in boiling water about 2 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain well, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and color loss.

beginner: Spinach is best right after you pick it and does not keep as long as tougher greens. Chill it quickly, use it within a week or so, and freeze any extra.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Spinach is more perishable than sturdier greens like kale, so chill it fast and use it within a week or so fresh; freezing is the best way to hold a glut from a fast spring or fall crop.

beginner: Spinach flowers (bolts) when the days get long and warm in late spring, and then the leaves turn bitter. To avoid it, plant as early as you can in spring, pick slow-bolting varieties, water steadily, and harvest before midsummer. The fall crop hardly bolts at all, which is why fall is the best time to grow spinach.
seasoned: Spinach bolts primarily in response to long days, so the spring window is short: sow as early as the soil can be worked, choose slow-bolting (long-standing) varieties, keep moisture and nitrogen steady, and harvest before the longest days of June. The fall crop, grown under shortening days, rarely bolts and is the main season; overwintered plants bolt in spring as days lengthen, so crop them before the flower stalk elongates.

beginner: Spinach bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns bitter) when days get long and warm. It is a normal part of its life cycle, not something you did wrong. The trick is to grow it in the cool, short-day parts of the year, especially fall.
seasoned: Bolting in spinach is mainly a long-day (photoperiod) response, with heat and drought speeding it; once the plant sends up a seed stalk the leaves turn bitter and tough. This is why spinach is grown as a fall, winter, and very-early-spring crop and the summer is left out across most regions.

beginner: For spring, pick slow-bolting kinds like Bloomsdale Long Standing or Tyee so the plants last longer before flowering. Melody and Space are easy, disease-resistant choices. For a fall or winter crop, grow a hardy type like Giant Winter. Smooth-leaf varieties are easiest to wash; the crinkly savoy types are the most cold-hardy but hold more grit.
seasoned: Match the variety to the slot. For the short spring window and any warm stretch, lean on slow-bolting (long-standing) types like Bloomsdale Long Standing, Tyee, and Olympia. Where downy mildew is a concern, choose resistant cultivars (Tyee, Melody, Space, and newer race-resistant hybrids). For fall and overwintering, the hardiest savoys (Giant Winter, Bloomsdale) take the most cold. Smooth-leaf types (Space, Olympia) wash easily and suit baby-leaf and containers; savoys are hardiest but trap grit; semi-savoys split the difference.

beginner: Spinach is often sown a bit thick, then thinned so plants stand about 3 to 4 inches apart. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby spinach. Thinning gives each plant room to grow full leaves.
seasoned: Sow a little thick and thin to 3 to 4 inches once plants have 3 to 4 true leaves; eat the thinnings as baby spinach. Crowded plants compete, stay small, and bolt sooner, and poor airflow invites downy mildew.

beginner: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach, which are all close relatives that share its pests and diseases.
seasoned: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach itself (all goosefoot-family hosts of the spinach leafminer, Fusarium wilt, and the leaf-mold diseases).

beginner: Do not plant spinach, beets, or chard in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between these related crops helps avoid the leafminer and soil diseases that build up in the ground.
seasoned: Rotate so spinach and its goosefoot relatives (beets, chard) do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years. The spinach leafminer overwinters as pupae in the soil and Fusarium wilt persists for years, so a long rotation away from the whole family is the core defense; deep spring cultivation also helps bury leafminer pupae.

beginner: In about 5 to 14 days the seeds sprout and push up two narrow seed leaves. Spinach comes up even in cold soil, but slowly.
seasoned: Seeds germinate in about 5 to 14 days, faster as soil warms toward 60 to 70°F and poorly above 75 to 85°F; two narrow cotyledons emerge.

beginner: Keep the soil damp and do not let it crust over. Cold soil means slower sprouting, which is normal.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist and uncrusted; expect slow but reliable emergence in cool soil and erratic germination in warm soil.

beginner: Have your spinach seeds come up yet?
seasoned: Did your spinach germinate, and how even is the stand?

beginner: The seedlings grow their first real spinach leaves. When they have 3 to 4 true leaves, it is time to thin them.
seasoned: Young plants form a low rosette; thin at the 3-to-4-true-leaf stage. Flea beetles and the first leafminer mines appear now.

beginner: Thin to about 3 to 4 inches apart and eat the thinnings. Watch for flea beetle holes and the first leafminer tunnels.
seasoned: Thin to 3 to 4 inches, keep moisture even, and set or check row cover to exclude leafminer flies.

beginner: How many true leaves do your seedlings have?
seasoned: Have you thinned, and is the row cover on?

beginner: The plants form a rosette of full-sized leaves. This is the main growing stage, when they build the leaves you will eat.
seasoned: Plants bulk a rosette of leaves over a few weeks; this is the productive window before bolt.

beginner: Keep them evenly watered and give one nitrogen feeding. Check the undersides of leaves for aphids and pick off any mined leaves.
seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen once, hold even moisture to delay bolt, and scout for aphids, leafminer, and downy mildew.

beginner: Is your spinach making lots of healthy leaves?
seasoned: Is the rosette filling out cleanly?

beginner: The leaves reach a usable size, about 3 to 6 inches long, dark green and tender. Pick before the plant starts to stretch upward.
seasoned: Leaves reach 3 to 6 inches at about 37 to 50 days (baby leaf earlier); harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again or cut the whole rosette above the crown for regrowth.

beginner: Pick the outer leaves, or cut the whole plant about an inch above the soil and let it regrow. Harvest in the cool morning.
seasoned: Crop frequently in the cool morning, taking outer leaves or whole-plant cuts; pick faster as days lengthen and warm to beat the bolt.

beginner: Have you started picking spinach?
seasoned: Are you harvesting, and is the plant still flat (not bolting)?

beginner: The center of the plant stretches up and starts to form a flower stalk, and the leaves turn bitter and arrow-shaped. This happens as the days get long and warm.
seasoned: The rosette elongates into a flowering stalk as days pass about 13 to 14 hours and warm; leaf flavor turns bitter and texture coarsens.

beginner: Spinach is a fast-growing, very cold-hardy leafy green grown in the cool parts of the year. It handles frost better than almost any other vegetable and can even live through winter under a cover to give you the first greens of spring. But it does not like heat and long summer days, which make it bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter quickly. That is why spinach grows best in fall and early spring, and why in hot places it is a winter crop. It comes in smooth-leaf types that are easy to wash and crinkly savoy types that are extra hardy, and it likes rich, moist soil that is not too acidic.
seasoned: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a fast, very cold-hardy leafy annual in the goosefoot family, grown for its tender, nutrient-dense leaves in the cool halves of the year. It is one of the hardiest garden vegetables, surviving hard frost into the low 20s°F and overwintering under snow or a row cover for the earliest spring harvest, yet it is also one of the quickest to bolt: lengthening days past about 13 to 14 hours, sped by heat and drought, send it to seed and turn the leaves bitter. That combination makes fall the main season nearly everywhere, with a short early-spring window and, in hot regions, a fall-through-spring winter crop. Spinach comes in three leaf types, smooth (flat), semi-savoy, and savoy (heavily crinkled), and is sensitive to acidic soil, preferring a near-neutral, fertile, evenly moist bed.
